SCDNR owned and managed lands are protected areas that play a critical role in conserving fish, wildlife, plants, and other natural and cultural resources. These lands are open to the public for a variety of recreational uses, from hunting and fishing to hiking and wildlife viewing.

SCDNR Public Lands FAQ
What can I do on SCDNR Lands?
SCDNR lands are managed for multiple uses and are available for everyone in South Carolina to enjoy. From hunting and fishing, to birding and wildlife viewing, to hiking, SCDNR lands provide access to outdoor recreation for everyone.
Hunting is allowed on Wildlife Management Areas. Depending on the property, certain activities may be restricted to protect the resources. Some properties are closed during certain dates for scheduled hunts and events. To find out what you can do where:
Check the property details page, accessed from the map above.
Review the annual Regulations Book.
Check the SCDNR properties regulations.
What kinds of lands does SCDNR manage?
Wildlife Management Areas (WMA) - WMAs are SCDNR owned or leased lands managed for wildlife, habitat and hunting. In addition to hunting, visitors may utilize these properties for other recreational opportunities, including wildlife viewing, hiking and birding.
Heritage Preserves - Lands dedicated to protecting significant natural and cultural resources such as rare species and important historic or pre-historic sites. Some Natural Heritage Preserves are also WMAs and allow hunting, others such as Cultural Heritage Preserves do not allow hunting.
Shooting Ranges - SCDNR operates both manned and unmanned shooting and archery ranges across the state.
State Lakes - State Lakes are managed to provide fishing opportunities to the public in areas of the state where the opportunity is lacking or where there are few public fishing lakes.
Other Managed Lands - Other SCDNR managed lands include fish hatcheries, research reserves, seabird sanctuaries, and more.
What types of WMAs are there?
Two types of property are included in the Wildlife Management Area Program: “specific” named WMAs and “other” unnamed WMAs. Other WMA lands occur as scattered tracts, often leased from private landowners and the forest industry. The hunting seasons and limits for these unnamed properties are set by Game Zone in which the property is located. “Specific” WMAs are generally larger tracts of land, many owned and managed by SCDNR. These properties often have additional restrictions and closures throughout each season for special hunts.
To promote hunting success, SCDNR also manages some WMAs for specific hunting opportunities. These areas include:
Public Dove Fields
Waterfowl Management Areas
Quail Focal Areas
Bird Dog Training Areas
What are Game Zones, and what do I need to know about them?
South Carolina hunting seasons, methods of harvest and limits are established by the SC General Assembly at the Game Zone level for both public Wildlife Management Areas and private lands. South Carolina currently has four game zones. It is important to know the regulations for the game zone where you are hunting.
See the map above and the annual Regulations for more details.

MAY FOREST STATE PARK
COAST
JAY REESE
PARK MANAGER
Welcome! My name is Jay Reese, and I am the park manager at May Forest State Park. As a kid growing up camping, fishing, exploring, hiking and learning to play golf in state parks, I was always SO excited to see a park ranger! When I was around 8 or 9 years-old, I received my Junior Forest Ranger hat and badge. I wore them all the time. Now I can proudly say, my Junior Forest Ranger hat and badge has been replaced with a South Carolina State Park hat and badge. My Junior Forest Ranger badge still sits on my desk reminding me of the amazing experiences I had as a kid and the lasting memories I am part of today!
One of my favorite spots at May Forest is sitting on the swing that sits on the bluff overlooking the Charleston Harbor. If you're a first-time visitor to the park, I would encourage you to take some time to experience the stunning view of the Charleston Harbor.
**Our Ultimate Outsider stamp is located outside the double doors of the chapel.
May Forest State Park is located on James Island at the end of Fort Johnson Road. The 23 acres, once owned by the Sisters of Charity of Our Lady of Mercy, is rich with history dating back to the Archaic Period. The property includes a canopy of live oaks, native plants and exotic vegetation. By far, the stand-out feature of May Forest is the stunning view of the Charleston Harbor, where visitors can see a beautiful perspective of Charleston. One can point out the famous Battery, the Cooper River Bridge, the Yorktown and all the way to Sullivan’s Island. Visitors can enjoy the serenity of this majestic property, take in the breathtaking scenery, picnic on the bluff, enjoy the screened gazebo or relax in a swing. Guests can also view a wide variety of wildlife, from catching a glimpse of dolphins playing in the harbor, coastal birds, raccoons and squirrels to name only a few.
While May Forest State Park is in a day-use only soft open phase, visitors can enjoy the serene property, and watch the park unfold into a spectacular event venue with overnight accommodations.
